result:
## Short answer

Yes — it's happened, at least three times in late 2025, and the CRM records the complaint but almost nothing about the response. The complaint was never about *who* the new person was; in every case it was about the account going silent during the handover.

## What's actually in the CRM

Four activities across three records. That's the entire evidence base.

| Date | Account | Type | Recorded content (verbatim, German) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-09-18 | Reply Deutschland | Inbound email from Katrin Sommer, subj. *Wechsel der Ansprechpartner* | "Der ständige Wechsel der Ansprechpartner ist für uns ein echtes Problem." |
| 2025-11-04 | valantic AG | Inbound email, no subject | "Nach dem Wechsel des Ansprechpartners kam fünf Tage lang keine Antwort." |
| 2025-11-04 | Körber Digital | Inbound email, no subject | "Nach dem Wechsel des Ansprechpartners kam fünf Tage lang keine Antwort." |
| 2025-12-03 | Reply Deutschland | Internal note, subj. *Post-mortem Betreuerwechsel* | "Der Kunde hat das im Oktober klar angesprochen; wir haben zu spät reagiert." |

**What happened:** Reply's complaint was about churn itself — *constant* changes, plural, so they had been through it more than once. valantic and Körber both reported the same specific failure: five days of no reply after the switch.

**How we reacted:** the only record of our response is our own post-mortem admitting we reacted too late. There is no logged recovery call, no escalation, no apology, no remediation plan, and no record of the outcome — I can't tell you from the CRM whether we kept any of these three accounts.

## Three caveats you should weigh before leaning on this

1. **These aren't the live accounts.** All three records are named "*Company* Betreuerwechsel" — they're case records about this topic, not the customer accounts themselves. There is no plain "Reply Deutschland" or "valantic AG" org in this workspace, and no deals, projects or tasks anywhere in it. So this is a curated file on the question, not the account history; the real relationship history lives somewhere I can't see.
2. **The two 4 November entries are word-for-word identical and both untitled.** That may be two customers saying the same thing, or one text duplicated across two records. I'd verify before citing "three separate incidents" to anyone.
3. **The post-mortem contradicts the timeline.** It says the customer raised it "in October"; the logged complaint is 18 September. Either an October escalation was never written down, or the post-mortem is misremembering — and if it's the former, the gap between complaint and reaction was longer than the file shows.

The workspace's semantic search is not working (it fell back to word matching and returned nothing), so I found these structurally. Given the workspace holds only seven organisations total, I'm confident I've seen everything here — but "everything here" is thin.

## What to be prepared for

Grounded in the pattern above:

- **The silence, not the swap, is what generates the complaint.** Two of three complaints name a specific number of days without an answer. Whatever else you do, the new manager must answer inbound mail same-day for the first few weeks — a slow reply in week one is the thing that becomes the escalation.
- **If this account has been through a change before, expect the "*ständige* Wechsel" reaction** — a sharper, relationship-level objection rather than an operational one. Check the account's own history for a prior handover before you announce this one.
- **Expect the complaint to arrive by email to whoever they last trusted**, and expect it to be read late. Reply's post-mortem is an admission that the signal was visible and nobody acted for weeks.

## What I'd learn from it

The recurring failure is ours, not the customer's: we changed the person and then didn't watch the account. Two things would have caught all three cases —

- a **named overlap period** where the outgoing manager stays on the thread rather than a clean cut-over, and
- an **explicit watch on response time** for the first 30 days, owned by someone other than the new manager.

One more thing worth knowing: every one of these records is owned by a user who is no longer on the active roster. So the person who ran these handovers has themselves left, with no successor recorded on the case files — which is how the learning got lost in the first place.

I've only read; I've written nothing and there's nothing waiting in your approvals queue. If it'd help, I can log the pattern as a note on the account you're about to change, or create the follow-up tasks for the overlap period and the 30-day response-time watch — say which account and I'll draft them for your approval.
